idiom_name: &mut String / &mut Vec<T> sink with write! (std::fmt::Write or std::io::Write)
implementation_notes: Rust realizes the pattern with an exclusive borrow of the accumulator: producers take `&mut String`/`&mut Vec<T>` and append with `write!`/`writeln!` through `std::fmt::Write` (implemented for `String`) or `std::io::Write` (implemented for `Vec<u8>`), or with `push_str`/`push`. The `Write` traits are the library-grade sink protocol: any producer written against `impl Write` can target a string, a byte vector, a file or a socket buffer. Because the borrow checker makes the mutation visible at the call site the accumulator form is safe but explicit - and when a single producer computes the whole result, returning an owned `String`/`Vec` (or an iterator finished with `.collect()`) is the idiomatic choice.
pitfalls: `write!` on a `String` returns a `Result` marked `must_use`: dropping it (a bare `write!(...);`) warns, and the error path disappears.
There is only one `&mut` at a time: holding the accumulator's borrow while calling a producer that also needs `&mut self` of the same struct does not compile - restructure or split the borrow.
`fmt::Write` and `io::Write` both provide `write_fmt`, so a module importing both needs `use std::fmt::Write as _;` or the `write!` call becomes ambiguous.
